claim: Telling clinicians to be slow and analytic does not raise diagnostic accuracy over telling them to be fast; case difficulty and experience matter far more.
note: Norman 2014 (two cohorts) and Ilgen 2013 (393 clinicians) are separate studies. Norman's n of 96/108 and '30% longer' not confirmed in the third round; the 44.5 vs 45.0 figure was seen twice. Sherbino r=-0.54 unverified. Matches our ARC and word-puzzle losses for forced slowing.

claim: Unstructured reflection on one's own first diagnosis rarely changes answers and corrects about as often as it breaks them.
note: Monteiro 2015: 8% revised, 1.20 to 1.22; only 18% of wrong answers revised. Lambe 2018: 16 corrections vs 26 backfires (short), 14 vs 14 (long); strict accuracy 0.42/0.41 vs 0.47 control. Human students and residents, not LLMs.

claim: Reflection can help in specific conditions: complex cases, cases resembling earlier ones, and delayed (not immediate) test performance; it does nothing on simple cases.
note: Mamede 2008/2010/2012 and the Lambe 2016 review favour structured reflection; Monteiro 2015, Lambe 2018 and Ilgen 2013 find nothing. Mamede lines are snippet-level only. Likely resolution: gains when reflection is structured and the case is hard, not by default. Supports a conditional trigger, not a schedule.

claim: Premature closure is the most common cognitive cause of diagnostic error in a 100-case internal-medicine series; knowledge gaps were rare.
note: All three lines are the same study (Graber 2005). Case series, no control, so it shows where errors cluster, not what fixes them. The earlier brief's 74%/65% were later reported as about three quarters and two thirds. Anchoring and overconfidence reviews (Saposnik 2016, Berner 2008) are related but rest on low-quality studies.

claim: A differential-diagnosis checklist raises accuracy only when it contains the correct diagnosis (0.75 vs 0.49); without it 0.43; a prompt to list own alternatives 0.53, not significant.
note: One RCT of 90 students (Kammer 2021), cited three times. Indirect support: Lambe 2018 students named the correct diagnosis among alternatives more often under lenient scoring but final accuracy did not rise. Key for design: an outside source of candidates, not a 'think of more' nag.

claim: Debiasing instruction and bias-focused checklists do not reliably reduce diagnostic error in controlled studies; knowledge-reorganizing strategies help a little.
note: Sibbald 2019 RCT (neither checklist beat control), Smith 2015 workshop (1 of 4 outcomes), Norman 2017 review, Tung 2022 review (preprint). The earlier brief's recalled claim that retrieval checklists beat debiasing was refuted. Norman 2009 essay (c-12) argued the opposite before the null trials.

claim: Physician confidence tracks case difficulty poorly, and overconfidence is linked to diagnostic error.
note: Meyer 2013: 55.3% vs 5.8% correct, confidence 7.2 vs 6.4. Saposnik review has mostly low-quality studies. Implication: self-reported confidence is a weak gate; use agreement or checks that read real input.

claim: Illness-script training has a theoretical basis but thin controlled evidence of better diagnosis.
note: Custers 2015 is a narrative review; Lee 2010 RCT shows 14% gain on reasoning problems but no change in overall diagnostic thinking (snippet). Schmidt and Boshuizen not retrieved. Treat illness-script cards as untested for LLMs.

claim: Giving physicians an LLM did not reliably beat the LLM alone: the LLM alone scored higher than physicians with the LLM in US, UK and ophthalmology studies.
note: Goh 2024 (76 vs 74, LLM alone 92); Healy 2026 UK (LLM alone 21 points higher); Ong 2026 (0.70 alone vs 0.60 assisted). Healy and Ong are 2026 abstracts, low credibility. Programs should use the model's output through structure, not leave it to a human to apply.

claim: The size of the human gain from LLM help is inconsistent: null in the US trial, positive in the UK replication and in two small 2026 studies, with some users harmed.
note: Goh +2 (P=.60); Healy +8.6 (p=.001); Ong +0.15 but 20% worse; Cusacovich top-3 up, top-1 not (p=.08). Different tasks, tiny n, abstract only. Wrong LLM advice was followed in a large share of failures (Ong 58.6%).

claim: GPT-4 put the final diagnosis in its differential 64% of the time (45/70) but ranked it first only 39% (27/70) on NEJM clinicopathologic cases.
note: One study (Kanjee 2023), three confirmations of the same numbers. Gap between 'in the list' and 'top-1' suggests recall is higher than ranking; supports generate-then-discriminate. Model is old; no newer replication found.

claim: Injecting cognitive-bias cues into medical questions lowers LLM accuracy, small open models most; bias-awareness prompts and few-shot recover only part.
note: BiasMedQA (npj Digit Med 2024) is one benchmark; independent support: Oh 2026 (models abandon correct reasoning given misleading expert hints) and Hager 2024 (sensitivity to information order and quantity). Reported drop sizes differ across lines (GPT-4 about 5%, worst 10 to 26%) because of averaging choices. Our model is small, so anchoring by a wrong card or hint is a real risk.

claim: MAI-DxO, an orchestrated panel around o3, reached about 80% (85.5% max) on 304 NEJM sequential cases vs 20% for generalist physicians, with lower cost; reported to hold across model families.
note: One non-peer-reviewed vendor preprint. Caveats: virtual costs, hard cases, physicians without references, simulated gatekeeper, no ablation separating structure from extra compute. The cross-model claim (b-13) was not independently checked.

claim: Medprompt (dynamic few-shot, self-generated CoT, choice-shuffle ensemble) lifted GPT-4 above 90% on MedQA with fewer calls than Med-PaLM 2's approach.
note: One preprint, exam-style benchmark; the abstract does not say which component carried the gain. Choice-shuffle is the one component that maps to an anti-anchoring step.

claim: Partial or badly configured reasoning schemas can score below no schema: removing any module dropped a TCM pipeline below zero-shot; poor LLM setups worsened physician decisions; a checklist without the right answer scored below control.
note: The two 2026 LLM items are low-credibility abstracts (40 and 50). The human Kammer arm (0.43 vs 0.49) was not significant. Consistent with our own scaffold losses but not strong independent proof.

claim: Frontier LLMs did worse than physicians on 2,400 real MIMIC-IV abdominal cases and did not follow guidelines, which contrasts with strong results on curated NEJM cases.
note: Hager 2024 versus curated-case results (Kanjee, MAI-DxO). Real, messy inputs versus published puzzle cases is the likely cause. Models tested were older. One real-data benchmark only.

claim: Longer reasoning in medical LLMs is not always better: non-reasoning models saturate quickly.
note: LLM side is one 2026 abstract (Oh); human side is Norman 2014. Different mechanisms, so not truly the same claim. Worth a delta check.

claim: Correction: PMC4539330 is Monteiro 2015, not Norman 2014; the Norman 2014 record is PubMed 24362377.
note: Three rounds agree (a, b, c). Fix the earlier brief's reference 2.

claim: Outpatient diagnostic error occurs in about 5% of US adult visits (about 12 million adults a year), about half potentially harmful.
note: Singh 2014, three observational studies pooled; abstract only. Context only, not a design input.

claim: AMIE, a conversational diagnostic LLM, was rated better than primary care physicians on most axes in a 159-scenario simulation.
note: Vendor study, simulated patients, text chat only; abstract only. Not about schema structure.
